labels.primary: row 4, with one cell left

frames.text: Row 4 has one empty cell, r4c9, and lacks only 8.

step.description: Full House: r4c9 is the last empty cell in row 4, so it must be 8.

labels.primary: the cell with one candidate left
labels.secondary: the other eight digits, each already in its row, column or box

frames.text: Only one candidate is left in r4c1: 1.
The row, column and box of r4c1 already hold the other eight digits.

step.description: Naked Single: the row, column and box of r4c1 already hold the other eight digits, so r4c1 must be 1.

labels.primary: row 2: 1 has one place left in it
labels.secondary: the 1s that rule out its other cells, shaded along their lines

frames.text: In row 2, the 1 can go only in r2c2.
The 1s in r4c1, r1c5 and r7c9 rule out 1 in every other empty cell of row 2.

step.description: Hidden Single: 1 fits only in r2c2 within row 2.

labels.primary: two cells that hold only 3 and 7 between them, in column 1 and box 1

frames.text: In column 1 and box 1, r1c1 and r2c1 hold only 3 and 7.

walk.lead: They must be 3 and 7, one each: these digits can go nowhere else in column 1 or box 1.

step.description: Locked Pair: in column 1 and box 1, r1c1 and r2c1 hold only 3 and 7, so these digits can go nowhere else in column 1 or box 1.

labels.primary: three cells that hold only 2, 3 and 7 between them, in row 8 and box 7

frames.text: In row 8 and box 7, r8c1, r8c2 and r8c3 hold only 2, 3 and 7 between them.

walk.lead: They must be 2, 3 and 7, one each: these digits can go nowhere else in row 8 or box 7.

step.description: Locked Triple: in row 8 and box 7, r8c1, r8c2 and r8c3 hold only 2, 3 and 7 between them, so these digits can go nowhere else in row 8 or box 7.

labels.primary: box 4: every 3 in it sits on one row
labels.secondary: row 5, which loses 3 outside box 4

frames.text: In box 4, the only cells that can take 3 are r5c1 and r5c3.
One of them must be 3, and both lie in row 5, so no other cell of row 5 can be 3.

step.description: Locked Candidates (Pointing): in box 4, every 3 lies in row 5, so no other cell of row 5 can be 3.

labels.primary: row 1: every 5 in it sits in one box
labels.secondary: box 2, which loses 5 outside row 1

frames.text: In row 1, the only cells that can take 5 are r1c5 and r1c6.
One of them must be 5, and both lie in box 2, so no other cell of box 2 can be 5.

step.description: Locked Candidates (Claiming): in row 1, every 5 lies in box 2, so no other cell of box 2 can be 5.

labels.primary: two cells that hold only 2 and 5 between them, in row 9

frames.text: In row 9, r9c2 and r9c7 hold only 2 and 5.

walk.lead: They must be 2 and 5, one each: these digits can go nowhere else in row 9.

step.description: Naked Pair: in row 9, r9c2 and r9c7 hold only 2 and 5, so these digits can go nowhere else in row 9.

labels.primary: three cells that hold only 2, 6 and 7 between them, in box 8

frames.text: In box 8, r7c4, r8c6 and r9c4 hold only 2, 6 and 7 between them.

walk.lead: They must be 2, 6 and 7, one each: these digits can go nowhere else in box 8.

step.description: Naked Triple: in box 8, r7c4, r8c6 and r9c4 hold only 2, 6 and 7 between them, so these digits can go nowhere else in box 8.

labels.primary: the only two cells of row 4 where 6 and 8 can go

frames.text: In row 4, the digits 6 and 8 can go only in r4c3 and r4c7.

walk.lead: They must be 6 and 8, one each, and hold nothing else: r4c3 and r4c7 keep only 6 and 8.

step.description: Hidden Pair: in row 4, the digits 6 and 8 can go only in r4c3 and r4c7, so these cells can hold nothing else.

labels.primary: the only three cells of row 8 where 3, 5 and 9 can go

frames.text: In row 8, the digits 3, 5 and 9 can go only in r8c4, r8c6 and r8c9.

walk.lead: They must be 3, 5 and 9, one each, and hold nothing else: r8c4 keeps only 3 and 5; r8c6 keeps only 3 and 9.

step.description: Hidden Triple: in row 8, the digits 3, 5 and 9 can go only in r8c4, r8c6 and r8c9, so these cells can hold nothing else.

labels.primary: four cells that hold only 5, 6, 8 and 9 between them, in row 5

frames.text: In row 5, r5c4, r5c5, r5c6 and r5c9 hold only 5, 6, 8 and 9 between them.

walk.lead: They must be 5, 6, 8 and 9, one each: these digits can go nowhere else in row 5.

step.description: Naked Quadruple: in row 5, r5c4, r5c5, r5c6 and r5c9 hold only 5, 6, 8 and 9 between them, so these digits can go nowhere else in row 5.

labels.primary: the only four cells of box 5 where 1, 2, 5 and 8 can go

frames.text: In box 5, the digits 1, 2, 5 and 8 can go only in r4c5, r4c6, r5c5 and r5c6.

walk.lead: They must be 1, 2, 5 and 8, one each, and hold nothing else: r4c5 keeps only 1 and 2; r4c6 keeps only 1 and 5; r5c5 keeps only 2 and 8.

step.description: Hidden Quadruple: in box 5, the digits 1, 2, 5 and 8 can go only in r4c5, r4c6, r5c5 and r5c6, so these cells can hold nothing else.

labels.primary: base rows: the 7s of the fish
labels.secondary: cover columns: 2 of them take the base's 7s, so 7 goes nowhere else in them

frames.text: In rows 3 and 8, the 7s lie only in r3c3, r3c8, r8c3 and r8c8.
These cells lie in columns 3 and 8. Each of rows 3 and 8 needs a 7, and no column holds two, so each of columns 3 and 8 gets its 7 from one of rows 3 and 8.

walk.lead: No other cell of columns 3 and 8 can be 7.

step.description: X-Wing on 7: in rows 3 and 8, the 7s lie only in columns 3 and 8 (r3c3, r3c8, r8c3, r8c8). Those 2 rows will use up 7 in those 2 columns, so 7 can go nowhere else in them.

labels.primary: base columns: the 9s of the fish
labels.secondary: cover rows: 3 of them take the base's 9s, so 9 goes nowhere else in them

frames.text: In columns 1, 4 and 8, the 9s lie only in r3c1, r5c1, r4c4, r5c4, r3c8 and r4c8.
These cells lie in rows 3, 4 and 5. Each of columns 1, 4 and 8 needs a 9, and no row holds two, so each of rows 3, 4 and 5 gets its 9 from one of columns 1, 4 and 8.

walk.lead: No other cell of rows 3, 4 and 5 can be 9.

step.description: Swordfish on 9: in columns 1, 4 and 8, the 9s lie only in rows 3, 4 and 5 (r3c1, r5c1, r4c4, r5c4, r3c8, r4c8). Those 3 columns will use up 9 in those 3 rows, so 9 can go nowhere else in them.

labels.primary: base rows: the 6s of the fish
labels.secondary: cover columns: 4 of them take the base's 6s, so 6 goes nowhere else in them

frames.text: In rows 2, 6, 8 and 9, the 6s lie only in r2c5, r2c9, r6c5, r6c8, r8c6, r8c9, r9c6 and r9c8.
These cells lie in columns 5, 6, 8 and 9. Each of rows 2, 6, 8 and 9 needs a 6, and no column holds two, so each of columns 5, 6, 8 and 9 gets its 6 from one of rows 2, 6, 8 and 9.

walk.lead: No other cell of columns 5, 6, 8 and 9 can be 6.

step.description: Jellyfish on 6: in rows 2, 6, 8 and 9, the 6s lie only in columns 5, 6, 8 and 9 (r2c5, r2c9, r6c5, r6c8, r8c6, r8c9, r9c6, r9c8). Those 4 rows will use up 6 in those 4 columns, so 6 can go nowhere else in them.

links.text: The cells r2c3, r2c5, r3c4, r5c5 and r6c4 hold only 3 and 5. Each line joins two of them that see each other: they cannot hold the same digit, so their 3s take opposite shades, and so do their 5s.
If dark purple is true, the 3 in r2c3 is true, and the 3 in r6c3 goes.
If light purple is true, the 3 in r6c4 is true, and the 3 in r6c3 goes. Either way it is false.

step.description: Remote Pair: the cells r2c3, r2c5, r3c4, r5c5 and r6c4 hold only 3 and 5. Two of them that see each other cannot hold the same digit, so their 3s take opposite shades of purple, and so do their 5s: either every dark purple candidate is true, or every light purple one is. The 3 in r6c3 sees a dark purple 3 in r2c3 and a light purple 3 in r6c4, so it is false either way.

labels.primary: the pair: only 5 and 6 in both cells, in different rows and boxes of rows 4-6
labels.secondary: box 4's 6s: all in the pair's rows
labels.fins: 5 in the pair: one of the two cells is 5

frames.text: r4c6 and r5c8 hold only 5 and 6, in different rows and boxes of rows 4-6.
In box 4, row 6 has no 6, so the box's 6 is in row 4 or row 5.
If box 4's 6 is in row 4, r4c6 cannot be 6 and is 5; if it is in row 5, r5c8 is 5. Either way one of the two is 5.

walk.lead: r4c9 and r5c6 see both pair cells.

step.description: Chute Remote Pair: r4c6 and r5c8 hold only 5 and 6, in different rows and boxes of rows 4-6. In box 4, row 6 (r6c1, r6c2, r6c3) has no 6, so the box's 6 is in row 4 or row 5, and the pair cell in that row cannot be 6: it is 5. One pair cell is therefore 5, so 5 is removed from every cell that sees both.

labels.primary: the one cell with three candidates; 3 is the extra
labels.secondary: its row, column and box, each holding 3 three times

frames.text: Every unsolved cell but r5c6 holds exactly two candidates; r5c6 holds three.
In row 5, column 6 and box 5, which meet at r5c6, 3 is a candidate in three cells each.

walk.lead: Without the 3 in r5c6, every unsolved cell would hold two candidates, each found twice in its row, column and box. That is a deadly pattern: every cell could take its other candidate at once, and the puzzle would have two solutions.

step.description: BUG+1: removing 3 from r5c6 would leave a bivalue grid with two solutions, so r5c6 must be 3.

labels.primary: the two strong links on 1

step.description: Skyscraper on 1: r2c3 and r2c7 are the only places for 1 in row 2, as are r9c3 and r9c9 in row 9, and r2c3 sees r9c3. If r2c7 is not 1, r2c3 is, so r9c3 is not, so r9c9 is: one of r2c7 and r9c9 is 1, and 1 is removed from every cell that sees both.

labels.primary: the two strong links on 8

step.description: 2-String Kite on 8: r1c6 and r1c8 are the only places for 8 in row 1, as are r3c4 and r7c4 in column 4, and r1c6 sees r3c4. If r1c8 is not 8, r1c6 is, so r3c4 is not, so r7c4 is: one of r1c8 and r7c4 is 8, and 8 is removed from every cell that sees both.

labels.primary: the two strong links on 2

step.description: Turbot Fish on 2: r5c7 and r9c7 are the only places for 2 in column 7, as are r7c6 and r9c5 in box 8, and r9c7 sees r9c5. If r5c7 is not 2, r9c7 is, so r9c5 is not, so r7c6 is: one of r5c7 and r7c6 is 2, and 2 is removed from every cell that sees both.

labels.primary: box 1: its 5s all lie in row 1 or column 2
labels.secondary: column 5: its only 5s are r1c5 and r6c5

step.description: Empty Rectangle on 5: in box 1 every 5 lies in row 1 or column 2, and r1c5 and r6c5 are the only 5s in column 5. If r6c5 is 5, r6c2 is not: they share row 6. If not, r1c5 is 5, so box 1 has no 5 in row 1; its 5 lies in column 2, which runs through r6c2, so again r6c2 is not 5. So 5 is removed from r6c2.

labels.primary: cells holding 4 and 6
labels.secondary: strong link on 4

step.description: W-Wing: r3c7 and r9c5 both hold 4/6; the strong link on 4 (r8c5–r8c7) forces one of them to be 6, removing 6 from cells seeing both.

labels.primary: the pivot and the digit each pincer shares with it
labels.secondary: 6 in each pincer

frames.text: The pivot r7c7 holds only 7 and 9.
If r7c7 is 7, the pincer r7c6 (only 6 and 7) must be 6.
If r7c7 is 9, the pincer r8c9 (only 6 and 9) must be 6.

walk.lead: Either way a pincer is 6; r7c8 and r8c6 see both.

step.description: XY-Wing: pivot r7c7 (7/9) with pincers r7c6 (6/7) and r8c9 (6/9); one pincer must be 6, so 6 is removed from cells seeing both.

labels.primary: the pivot's 5 and 9, and the one each pincer shares with it
labels.secondary: 4 in all three cells

frames.text: The pivot r2c5 holds only 4, 5 and 9.
If r2c5 is 5, the pincer r3c6 (only 4 and 5) must be 4.
If r2c5 is 9, the pincer r7c5 (only 4 and 9) must be 4.

walk.lead: Or the pivot is 4 itself. Whichever digit it takes, one of the three cells is 4; r3c5 sees all three.

step.description: XYZ-Wing: pivot r2c5 (4/5/9) with pincers r3c6 (4/5) and r7c5 (4/9). Whichever digit the pivot takes, one of the three cells is 4, so 4 is removed from every cell that sees all three.

labels.primary: the bivalue cell and the three cells in box 5
labels.secondary: the 4s: at least one of them is true

frames.text: The bivalue cell r4c3 holds only 4 and 9.
The three cells r4c4, r5c5 and r6c5 in box 5 hold only 1, 4, 7 and 9 between them: one digit more than cells.
If r4c3 is 9, none of the three cells can be 9 (it sees the 9 in r4c4), so they must be 1, 4 and 7, and r5c5 is 4.

walk.lead: Either way r4c3 or r5c5 is 4; r4c6 and r5c3 see both.

step.description: WXYZ-Wing: bivalue cell r4c3 (4/9) and the three cells r4c4, r5c5 and r6c5 in box 5, which hold 1/4/7/9 between them. The 9 in r4c3 sees every 9 in the three cells. Either r4c3 is 4, or it is 9 and the three cells in box 5 must be 1, 4 and 7. At least one of the four cells is therefore 4, so 4 is removed from every other cell that sees all the 4s among them.

labels.primary: the three corners holding only 5/8
labels.secondary: 5 and 8 in the fourth corner: either would complete the deadly pattern

frames.text: Three corners of a rectangle, r4c1, r5c1 and r5c8, hold only 5 and 8.
The fourth corner, r4c8, holds 5 and 8 as well, and other digits too.

walk.lead: If r4c8 were 5 or 8, all four corners would hold only 5 and 8; they could swap, and the puzzle would have two solutions.

step.description: Unique Rectangle Type 1: r4c1, r4c8, r5c1, r5c8 would form a deadly pattern on 5/8; r4c8 cannot be 5 or 8.

labels.primary: the rectangle: 4/7 in all four corners
labels.secondary: 6, the roof's extra candidate: one of the two roof cells must be it

frames.text: 4 and 7 are candidates in all four corners of the rectangle: the floor, r5c2 and r6c2, holds only these two, and the roof, r5c4 and r6c4, holds other digits too.
Each of r5c4 and r6c4 holds just one other digit, the same one: 6.

walk.lead: If neither r5c4 nor r6c4 were 6, all four corners would hold only 4 and 7; they could swap, and the puzzle would have two solutions. One of them must therefore be 6, and r4c4 sees both.

step.description: Unique Rectangle Type 2: to avoid the deadly pattern on 4/7, one of r5c4/r6c4 must be 6, so 6 is removed from cells seeing both.

labels.primary: the rectangle: 7/8 in all four corners
labels.secondary: 1 and 6: the roof's extras (r7c4, r7c5, read as one cell) and r7c6 hold only these in row 7, a naked pair

frames.text: 7 and 8 are candidates in all four corners of the rectangle: the floor, r3c4 and r3c5, holds only these two, and the roof, r7c4 and r7c5, holds other digits too.
The roof's extras are 1 and 6, and r7c6, also in row 7, holds only 1 and 6.

walk.lead: If neither roof cell took one of its extras, all four corners would hold only 7 and 8; they could swap, and the puzzle would have two solutions. A roof cell must therefore take one of its extras, and, read as one cell, the roof makes a naked pair with r7c6: 1 and 6 can go nowhere else in row 7.

step.description: Unique Rectangle Type 3: r3c4, r3c5, r7c4, r7c5 would form a deadly pattern on 7/8, so one of the roof cells r7c4, r7c5 must take an extra candidate. Read as one cell holding its extras (1 and 6), the roof makes a naked pair with r7c6 in row 7: 1 and 6 can only go in these cells, so they are removed from the rest of row 7.

labels.primary: the rectangle: 4/6 in all four corners
labels.secondary: 6 in column 9: only in the roof, so one of r2c9, r8c9 is 6

frames.text: 4 and 6 are candidates in all four corners of the rectangle: the floor, r2c7 and r8c7, holds only these two, and the roof, r2c9 and r8c9, holds other digits too.
In column 9, 6 is a candidate only in the roof, so r2c9 or r8c9 is 6.

walk.lead: If r2c9 or r8c9 were 4, the other would be 6, and all four corners would hold only 4 and 6; they could swap, and the puzzle would have two solutions.

step.description: Unique Rectangle Type 4: 6 is locked into r2c9/r8c9; keeping 4 there would force the deadly pattern, so 4 is removed from r2c9 and r8c9.

labels.primary: the rectangle: 4/8 in all four corners
labels.secondary: 5 in the roof cells: one of them must be it

frames.text: 4 and 8 are candidates in all four corners of the rectangle: r5c8 holds only these two, and r5c9, r8c8 and r8c9 hold other digits too.
Each of r5c9, r8c8 and r8c9 holds just one other digit, the same one: 5.

walk.lead: If none of r5c9, r8c8 and r8c9 were 5, all four corners would hold only 4 and 8; they could swap, and the puzzle would have two solutions. One of them must therefore be 5, and r9c9 sees all of them.

step.description: Unique Rectangle Type 5: one of r5c9, r8c8, r8c9 must be 5 to avoid the deadly pattern, so 5 is removed from cells seeing all of them.

labels.primary: the rectangle: 5/6 in all four corners
labels.secondary: 6 in rows 5 and 6: only in the rectangle, so on one diagonal

frames.text: 5 and 6 are candidates in all four corners of the rectangle: the floor, r5c6 and r6c9, holds only these two, and the roof, r5c9 and r6c6, holds other digits too.
Rows 5 and 6 have 6 only in the rectangle, so their two 6s lie on the same diagonal.

walk.lead: If r5c9 or r6c6 were 6, both would be, and r5c6 and r6c9 would both be 5: all four corners would hold only 5 and 6; they could swap, and the puzzle would have two solutions.

step.description: Unique Rectangle Type 6: 6 is confined to the rectangle in both rows; placing it in a roof corner would force the deadly pattern, so 6 is removed from r5c9, r6c6.

labels.primary: the rectangle: 3/5 in all four corners
labels.secondary: 5 in row 6 and in column 5: only in the rectangle

frames.text: 3 and 5 are candidates in all four corners of the rectangle, and r9c6 holds only these two.
In row 6 and in column 5, which cross at r6c5, 5 is a candidate only in the rectangle.

walk.lead: If r6c5 were 3, row 6 would have its 5 in r6c6 and column 5 its 5 in r9c5, so r9c6, which sees both, would be 3: all four corners would hold only 3 and 5; they could swap, and the puzzle would have two solutions.

step.description: Hidden Rectangle: r9c6 holds only 3/5, and 5 is confined to the rectangle in r6c5's row and column; r6c5 cannot be 3 or the deadly pattern appears.

labels.primary: the three solved corners, none of them a given
labels.secondary: the cell that would complete the rectangle with 2

frames.text: Three corners of a rectangle are solved, none of them a given: r2c7 and r7c9 are 3, and r7c7 is 2.
The fourth corner, r2c9, still has 2 as a candidate.

walk.lead: If r2c9 were 2, all four corners would hold only 2 and 3, none of them a given; they could swap, and the puzzle would have two solutions.

step.description: Avoidable Rectangle Type 1: setting r2c9 to 2 would complete an interchangeable rectangle of solved (non-given) cells, contradicting the puzzle's unique solution.

labels.primary: the two solved corners, neither of them a given, and the 4 and 5 that would complete the rectangle
labels.secondary: 3 in the two unsolved corners: one of them must be it

frames.text: Two corners of a rectangle are solved, neither of them a given: r6c3 is 5 and r9c3 is 4; of the other two, r6c2 could be 4 and r9c2 could be 5.
Each of r6c2 and r9c2 holds just one other digit, the same one: 3.

walk.lead: If neither r6c2 nor r9c2 were 3, they would be 4 and 5, and all four corners would hold only 4 and 5, none of them a given; they could swap, and the puzzle would have two solutions. One of them must therefore be 3, and r7c2 sees both.

step.description: Avoidable Rectangle Type 2: to avoid an interchangeable rectangle with the solved cells r6c3, r9c3, one of r6c2/r9c2 must be 3, so 3 is removed from cells seeing both.

labels.primary: the cells that would form a deadly 2/4/9 loop
labels.secondary: 4 and 9 in r9c5: each would complete the deadly loop

frames.text: In rows 8 and 9, across three boxes, r8c1, r9c1, r8c5, r8c9 and r9c9 hold only 2, 4 and 9.
The sixth cell, r9c5, holds 4 and 9 as well, and other digits too.

walk.lead: If r9c5 were 4 or 9, all six cells would hold only 2, 4 and 9. Swapping the two cells in each of columns 1, 5 and 9 at once would then give a second solution.

step.description: Extended Rectangle Type 1: r8c1, r9c1, r8c5, r9c5, r8c9, r9c9 would form a deadly 2/4/9 loop; r9c5 must take one of its extra candidates.

labels.primary: base columns: the 8s of the fish
labels.secondary: cover rows: where the base columns put their 8s if the fin is false
labels.fins: fin: an 8 of the base columns outside the fish
labels.finBox: the fin's box: if the fin is true, no other cell here can be 8

frames.text: In columns 3 and 9, the 8s lie in r5c3, r8c3, r5c9 and r8c9, and in one more cell.
The only other 8 in columns 3 and 9 is r4c3: the fin.
If the fin is false, columns 3 and 9 put their 8s in rows 5 and 8, one in each, so no other cell of those rows can be 8.
If the fin is true, it is the 8 of box 4, so no other cell of box 4 can be 8.

walk.lead: r5c1 is in row 5 and in box 4, so it cannot be 8 either way.

step.description: Finned X-Wing on 8: in columns 3 and 9, the 8s lie in rows 5 and 8 (r5c3, r8c3, r5c9, r8c9) except for the fin r4c3. Either the fin is false and the fish holds, or the fin is true; an 8 that sees every fin and lies in the cover rows outside the base is false both ways.

labels.primary: base columns: the 1s of the fish
labels.secondary: cover rows: where the base columns put their 1s if every fin is false
labels.fins: fins: 1s of the base columns outside the fish
labels.finBox: the fins' box: if a fin is true, no other cell here can be 1

frames.text: In columns 4 and 8, the 1s lie in r6c4, r6c8 and r9c8, and in 2 more cells.
The only other 1s in columns 4 and 8 are r7c4 and r8c4: the fins.
The fish's corner r9c4 has no 1: the fins r7c4 and r8c4 stand in for it. If every fin is false, columns 4 and 8 put their 1s in rows 6 and 9, one in each, so no other cell of those rows can be 1.
If a fin is true, it is the 1 of box 8, so no other cell of box 8 can be 1.

walk.lead: r9c6 is in row 9 and in box 8, so it cannot be 1 either way.

step.description: Sashimi X-Wing on 1: in columns 4 and 8, the 1s lie in rows 6 and 9 (r6c4, r6c8, r9c8) except for the fins r7c4, r8c4. Either the fins are false and the fish holds, or a fin is true; a 1 that sees every fin and lies in the cover rows outside the base is false both ways.

labels.primary: base rows: the 3s of the fish
labels.secondary: cover columns: where the base rows put their 3s if the fin is false
labels.fins: fin: a 3 of the base rows outside the fish
labels.finBox: the fin's box: if the fin is true, no other cell here can be 3

frames.text: In rows 2, 3 and 7, the 3s lie in r2c2, r2c4, r3c4, r3c7, r7c4 and r7c7, and in one more cell.
The only other 3 in rows 2, 3 and 7 is r7c3: the fin.
If the fin is false, rows 2, 3 and 7 put their 3s in columns 2, 4 and 7, one in each, so no other cell of those columns can be 3.
If the fin is true, it is the 3 of box 7, so no other cell of box 7 can be 3.

walk.lead: r8c2 is in column 2 and in box 7, so it cannot be 3 either way.

step.description: Finned Swordfish on 3: in rows 2, 3 and 7, the 3s lie in columns 2, 4 and 7 (r2c2, r2c4, r3c4, r3c7, r7c4, r7c7) except for the fin r7c3. Either the fin is false and the fish holds, or the fin is true; a 3 that sees every fin and lies in the cover columns outside the base is false both ways.

labels.primary: base rows: the 1s of the fish
labels.secondary: cover columns: where the base rows put their 1s if the fin is false
labels.fins: fin: a 1 of the base rows outside the fish
labels.finBox: the fin's box: if the fin is true, no other cell here can be 1

frames.text: In rows 5, 6 and 8, the 1s lie in r5c3, r5c7, r6c5, r8c5 and r8c7, and in one more cell.
The only other 1 in rows 5, 6 and 8 is r6c2: the fin.

Row 6 has only one 1 in columns 3, 5 and 7, in r6c5: the fin r6c2 stands in for a second 1. If the fin is false, rows 5, 6 and 8 put their 1s in columns 3, 5 and 7, one in each, so no other cell of those columns can be 1.
If the fin is true, it is the 1 of box 4, so no other cell of box 4 can be 1.

walk.lead: r4c3 is in column 3 and in box 4, so it cannot be 1 either way.

step.description: Sashimi Swordfish on 1: in rows 5, 6 and 8, the 1s lie in columns 3, 5 and 7 (r5c3, r5c7, r6c5, r8c5, r8c7) except for the fin r6c2. Either the fin is false and the fish holds, or the fin is true; a 1 that sees every fin and lies in the cover columns outside the base is false both ways.

labels.primary: base rows: the 1s of the fish
labels.secondary: cover columns: where the base rows put their 1s if the fin is false
labels.fins: fin: a 1 of the base rows outside the fish
labels.finBox: the fin's box: if the fin is true, no other cell here can be 1

frames.text: In rows 1, 4, 7 and 8, the 1s lie in r1c1, r1c4, r4c1, r4c8, r7c3, r7c4, r8c3 and r8c8, and in one more cell.
The only other 1 in rows 1, 4, 7 and 8 is r4c7: the fin.
If the fin is false, rows 1, 4, 7 and 8 put their 1s in columns 1, 3, 4 and 8, one in each, so no other cell of those columns can be 1.
If the fin is true, it is the 1 of box 6, so no other cell of box 6 can be 1.

walk.lead: r5c8 is in column 8 and in box 6, so it cannot be 1 either way.

step.description: Finned Jellyfish on 1: in rows 1, 4, 7 and 8, the 1s lie in columns 1, 3, 4 and 8 (r1c1, r1c4, r4c1, r4c8, r7c3, r7c4, r8c3, r8c8) except for the fin r4c7. Either the fin is false and the fish holds, or the fin is true; a 1 that sees every fin and lies in the cover columns outside the base is false both ways.

labels.primary: base rows: the 6s of the fish
labels.secondary: cover columns: where the base rows put their 6s if the fin is false
labels.fins: fin: a 6 of the base rows outside the fish
labels.finBox: the fin's box: if the fin is true, no other cell here can be 6

frames.text: In rows 3, 4, 7 and 8, the 6s lie in r3c1, r4c2, r4c4, r7c2, r7c9, r8c1 and r8c9, and in one more cell.
The only other 6 in rows 3, 4, 7 and 8 is r3c6: the fin.

Row 3 has only one 6 in columns 1, 2, 4 and 9, in r3c1: the fin r3c6 stands in for a second 6. If the fin is false, rows 3, 4, 7 and 8 put their 6s in columns 1, 2, 4 and 9, one in each, so no other cell of those columns can be 6.
If the fin is true, it is the 6 of box 2, so no other cell of box 2 can be 6.

walk.lead: r1c4 is in column 4 and in box 2, so it cannot be 6 either way.

step.description: Sashimi Jellyfish on 6: in rows 3, 4, 7 and 8, the 6s lie in columns 1, 2, 4 and 9 (r3c1, r4c2, r4c4, r7c2, r7c9, r8c1, r8c9) except for the fin r3c6. Either the fin is false and the fish holds, or the fin is true; a 6 that sees every fin and lies in the cover columns outside the base is false both ways.

labels.primary: 2 and 6 in row 9: one in r9c4, the other where it meets box 9
labels.secondary: 4 and 7 in box 9: one in r7c7, the other where it meets row 9
labels.fins: 8: where row 9 meets box 9, so in both

frames.text: In row 9, r9c4 holds only 2 and 6. Whichever it is, r9c7, r9c8 and r9c9 can take at most one of 2 and 6.
The three cells are in box 9 too, where r7c7 holds only 4 and 7, so they can take at most one of 4 and 7 as well.
Their only other digit is 8, which they can take at most once. Three cells need three digits, so they hold one of 2 and 6, one of 4 and 7, and the 8.

walk.lead: Then r9c4 and the three cells hold both 2 and 6, r7c7 and the three cells both 4 and 7, and the three cells the 8.

step.description: Sue de Coq: r9c7, r9c8 and r9c9, in both row 9 and box 9, hold only 2, 4, 6, 7 and 8. r9c4 in row 9 takes 2 or 6, and r7c7 in box 9 takes 4 or 7, so the three cells hold one of 2 and 6, one of 4 and 7, and the 8. The other cells of row 9 outside box 9 lose 2, 6 and 8, and those of box 9 outside row 9 lose 4, 7 and 8.

links.text: Each line joins the only two 4s of a house: exactly one of them is true, so they take opposite shades. Either every dark purple 4 is true, or every light purple one is.
If dark purple is true, the 4 in r6c4 is true, and the 4 in r6c8 goes.
If light purple is true, the 4 in r8c8 is true, and the 4 in r6c8 goes. Either way it is false.

step.description: Simple Colors on 4: where a row, column or box has only two 4s, they take opposite shades of purple, so either every dark purple 4 is true or every light purple one is. The 4 in r6c8 sees a dark purple 4 in r6c4 and a light purple 4 in r8c8, so it is false either way.

links.text: Each line joins the only two 6s of a house: exactly one of them is true, so they take opposite shades. Either every dark purple 6 is true, or every light purple one is.
Another cluster of 6s, shaded the same way in orange: either every dark orange 6 is true, or every light orange one is.
The dark orange 6 in r9c8 and the dark purple 6 in r8c7 see each other (the dashed line), so they cannot both be true: light orange or light purple is true.
If light purple is true, the 6 in r8c6 is true, and the 6 in r3c6 goes.
If light orange is true, the 6 in r2c4 is true, and the 6 in r3c6 goes. Light orange or light purple is true, so it is false either way; one more 6 falls the same way.

step.description: Multi Colors on 6: two clusters of 6s are shaded, one purple and one orange; in each, where a row, column or box has only two 6s, they take opposite shades. The dark orange 6 in r9c8 and the dark purple 6 in r8c7 see each other, so they cannot both be true: light orange or light purple is true. The 6 in r3c6 sees a light purple 6 in r8c6 and a light orange 6 in r2c4, so it is false either way; one more 6 falls the same way.

links.text: Each line joins the only two places for a digit in a row, column or box; a cell with only two candidates joins those two, side by side (no line inside a cell). Exactly one of two joined candidates is true, so they take opposite shades: either every dark purple candidate is true, or every light purple one is.
If dark purple is true, the 1 in r7c3 is true, and the 1 in r7c2 goes.
If light purple is true, the 1 in r7c1 is true, and the 1 in r7c2 goes. Either way it is false.

step.description: 3D Medusa: where a row, column or box has only two places for a digit, or a cell has only two candidates, the two take opposite shades of purple, so either every dark purple candidate is true or every light purple one is. The 1 in r7c2 sees a dark purple 1 in r7c3 and a light purple 1 in r7c1, so it is false either way.

labels.primary: the chain on 1

step.description: X-Chain on 1: r8c3 → r8c6 → r6c6 → r6c7 → r4c8 → r9c8; one end must be 1, so 1 is removed from cells seeing both ends.

labels.primary: the loop on 2, with grouped nodes

step.description: Grouped X-Cycle on 2: a continuous loop through 6 nodes (groups included); along each weak link one side is 2, so 2 falls from outside cells seeing both sides.

labels.primary: the chain of bivalue cells

step.description: XY-Chain: r1c6 → r5c6 → r5c7 → r2c7; whichever way the chain resolves, one end is 4, so 4 is removed from cells seeing both ends.

labels.primary: the loop

step.description: Nice Loop: the continuous loop 3@r1c4 → 4@r1c4 → 4@r6c4 → 4@r6c5 → 3@r6c5 → 3@r2c5 alternates perfectly; every weak link has exactly one true side, clearing other candidates along it.

labels.primary: the loop, with grouped nodes

step.description: Grouped Nice Loop: the continuous loop 7@r1c8 → 9@r1c8 → 9@[r1c9, r2c9, r3c9] → 9@r5c9 → 8@r5c9 → 8@r9c9 → 7@r9c9 → 7@[r1c9, r2c9, r3c9] alternates perfectly; every weak link has exactly one true side, clearing candidates along it.

ALS-XZ: sets A (r8c2, r9c1) and B (r7c8, r8c9) each hold one digit more than they have cells, and every 1 of A sees every 1 of B, so at most one of them keeps a 1. The other loses its 1, its other digits fill its cells, and it holds a 5: A or B holds a 5, so 5 is removed from every cell that sees every 5 of both.

ALS-XY-Wing: the wings A (r8c3, r8c8) and B (r4c9, r6c8) and the hinge C (r6c3) each hold one digit more than they have cells; every 4 of C sees every 4 of A, and every 6 of C every 6 of B. C lacks at most one of its digits, so it holds a 4 (and A then holds no 4) or a 6 (and B then holds no 6). That wing's other digits fill its cells, and it holds a 7: A or B holds a 7, so 7 is removed from every cell that sees every 7 of both.

ALS-XY-Chain: sets A (r4c2, r4c7), B (r1c7), C (r1c5, r1c6) and D (r7c5) each hold one digit more than they have cells, linked by 9, 3 and 9: every 9 of A sees every 9 of B, every 3 of B every 3 of C, and every 9 of C every 9 of D. If A holds no 4, its other digits fill its cells, so it holds a 9; then B holds no 9 and holds a 3, C no 3 and a 9, and D no 9 and a 4: each set in turn loses its link digit and fills its cells. A or D holds a 4, so 4 is removed from every cell that sees every 4 of both.

labels.primary: the chain

step.description: AIC: 8@r1c6 → 4@r1c6 → 4@r5c6 → 2@r5c6 → 2@r5c9 → 2@r1c9; at least one of 8@r1c6 and 2@r1c9 is true, so candidates conflicting with both are removed.
Grouped AIC: 8@r1c2 → 4@r1c2 → 4@r1c1 → 4@r7c1 → 4@r7c5 → 4@r8c5 → 8@r8c5 → 8@[r8c6, r9c6]; at least one end is true, so candidates conflicting with both ends are removed.
AIC with ALS: 8@r2c9 → 8@r2c8 → 8@[r7c8, r8c8] → 9@[r7c8, r8c8] → 9@r6c8 → 9@r6c9; at least one end is true, so candidates conflicting with both ends are removed.

labels.primary: 4 in every petal: whichever digit the stem takes, a petal holds a 4
labels.secondary: the stem's candidates, and each petal's digit the stem sees

step.description: Death Blossom: the stem r8c9 holds 2, 5 and 7, and each has a petal, an almost locked set whose copies of that digit all see the stem: A (r9c7) for 2, B (r8c5, r9c6) for 5 and C (r8c1) for 7. Whichever digit the stem takes, its petal loses that digit, fills its cells with its other digits and holds a 4, so 4 is removed from every cell that sees every 4 of every petal.

labels.primary: the cross and its two wings: the only cells 1/4/8 can land on

step.description: Fireworks: digits 1/4/8 each must land on one of r8c6 (cross), r8c3 (row wing) or r2c6 (column wing), locking those three cells, so all other candidates there are removed.

labels.primary: the aligned pair
labels.secondary: the almost locked sets both cells see, which rule out pairings

step.description: Aligned Pair Exclusion: every candidate pairing of r7c4 and r8c4 that survives the sets they both see leaves no place for the removed candidate.

labels.primary: the base cells, holding 2/5/6
labels.secondary: the target cells: the base digits must land here

step.description: Exocet: base r9c8, r9c9 (2/5/6) with targets r7c3 and r8c5: a complete placement analysis proves the base digits must land in the targets, so the targets keep only base candidates.

labels.primary: cells no complete placement of 9 uses

step.description: Pattern Overlay: of the 6 complete placements possible for digit 9, none uses r9c1.

links.text: r1c1 = 8, so 3 is removed from r1c1.
If r1c1 is not 8, then r1c3 must be 8: the only place left for 8 in row 1.
r1c3 = 8, then r8c4 must be 8: the only place left for 8 in row 8.
r8c4 = 8, then r9c4 must be 4: the only place left for 4 in column 4.
r9c4 = 4, then r7c4 must be 6: the only place left for 6 in box 8.
r7c4 = 6, then r9c9 must be 6: the only place left for 6 in box 9.
r9c9 = 6, then r2c6 must be 6: the only place left for 6 in row 2.
r2c6 = 6, then r1c6 must be 3: the only place left for 3 in column 6.
r1c6 = 3, so 3 is removed from r1c1.

labels.primary: r1c1 = 8 and its opposite, each followed along its own line to the same conclusion

step.description: Digit forcing: whether r1c1 is 8 or not, the forced singles agree on the same conclusions.

links.text: r1c4 = 4, then r1c2 must be 9: the only candidate left in r1c2.
r1c2 = 9, then r5c2 must be 2: the only candidate left in r5c2.
r5c2 = 2, then r6c2 must be 7: the only candidate left in r6c2.
r6c2 = 7, then r6c9 must be 2: the only candidate left in r6c9.
r6c9 = 2, then r4c6 must be 2: the only place left for 2 in row 4.
r4c6 = 2, then r4c7 must be 4: the only place left for 4 in row 4.
r4c7 = 4, then row 4 would have no place left for 7: a contradiction.

labels.primary: the assumption and the singles it forces: one line of the reasoning, read along the arrows
labels.secondary: the house that would be left with no place for a digit

step.description: Nishio: assuming r1c4 = 4 and following the forced singles leads to a contradiction, so 4 is impossible there.
